doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

chapter: Papa Jo Jones and the Sweet Baby Blues Band
title: Papa Jo Jones as mentor and houseguest
summary: Retirement homes for musicians lead to Papa Jo Jones, who mentored Jimmy, turned up at his concerts and stayed with them until Jeannie made him smoke outside.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Well they did, they had this big apartment building in New York City for musicians that retired and stuff. And Dizzy Gillespie I think had this hospital set up where he could go and get treatments or something, down in New Jersey somewhere. But that’s sort of like what I’m speaking of. Because that we speak a different language. And so when we get put out to pasture, we should be around people that have done what we have done.

Like she said, one of the saddest things, like was when Papa Jo Jones was like a mentor you see and everything. I mean he raised me professionally and everything. And wherever we went after we left New York, and I was called to Bennington to teach and then Wisconsin and finally L.A. But the thing is is that he would show up at my first concert, wherever I held it. And nobody’d tell him.
He’d just be sitting there backstage there in the chair with his handkerchief.
Yeah. I’d come in and he’d be there. Fantastic. What an inspiration you know, to have that kind of back-up.
Really it makes you feel very special.
And then, as we moved, wherever we would come, he knew and we’d tell him, look Jo, whenever you feel out of sorts, where we are, you’ve got a home.
And he came and stayed with us many a time.

And sometime he’d stay one week or two weeks, or sometimes a day, bing and he’s gone, or he’s going to see some other musicians like up in San Diego then go to L.A., that type of thing, make his rounds.

He told everybody I put him out because I wouldn’t let him smoke. Well, he was a chain smoker. And I told him I said, “Jo Jones, you’re going to have to go out on the patio and smoke.” And so he went back to New York and we got calls all week long, “You threw Jo Jones out?” “You put Papa Jo out?” I said yes we did.
And then when we got to New York and everything, everybody was still talking about it.

He told everybody I put him out. But he was smoking too much. Because I had a bronchial thing, and I’m trying to sing too, and so I was really getting that second hand smoke then you know. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
